content.title: About
content.content: Canola oil is extracted from the seeds of the rapeseed plant (Brassica napus). It has a light yellow color, neutral taste, and a high smoke point, making it popular for frying, baking, and salad dressings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rapeseed is one of the most widely cultivated oilseed crops worldwide.
Compared with traditional rapeseed oil, canola oil has low erucic acid and glucosinolate levels.
Canola was developed in Canada in the 1970s through selective breeding to improve its nutritional profile.
Rapeseed oil is frequently used in the production of biodiesel.
After oil extraction, the remaining rapeseed meal serves as high‑protein animal feed.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Canola oil contains alpha‑linolenic acid (ALA), which supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Less than 7 % of the fat in canola oil is saturated, helping to lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Supports skin health
items.content: Easily absorbed fatty acids help moisturize and maintain the skin barrier.

items.title: Contains phytosterols
items.content: Phytosterols may aid in reducing blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Rapeseed allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to canola oil.

items.title: Thermal stability
items.content: Overheating can cause the formation of trans fats; stay within the recommended smoke point.

items.title: Glucosinolate content
items.content: Improperly processed oil may retain trace glucosinolates, which are undesirable in large amounts.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Canola oil is suitable for frying, baking, making sauces, and dressing salads. Its neutral flavor makes it a versatile ingredient in recipes where a strong oil taste is not desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the oil in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated to slow oxidation. Discard the oil if it develops a rancid smell or becomes cloudy.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg salad is a classic dish made from hard‑boiled eggs mixed with a fat‑free dressing (such as yogurt, kefir or mustard). In 1963 this low‑calorie version became popular as a light and nutritious snack or meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the oldest human food sources.
During the 1960s, fat‑free dressings started to replace mayonnaise to lower dish calories.
Egg salad is often served on bread, in lettuce cups, or as a side to vegetables.
Different countries add distinct spices: the US often uses celery and dill, while Russia prefers mustard and green onion.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: The yolk is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using a fat‑free dressing reduces the overall saturated fat content of the dish.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Choline supports liver function and the nervous system.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and a small amount of fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites or yolks.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improperly cooked or stored eggs can harbor Salmonella.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: While nutritious, egg yolks contain cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve egg salad cold, as a sandwich filling, in lettuce cups, or alongside vegetable dishes. Fresh herbs, cucumber, radish or capers can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: The sausage biscuit sandwich is a quick snack consisting of a grilled or boiled sausage placed between two halves of a soft biscuit (American style). It is often served hot, sometimes with mustard, ketchup or melted cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century as convenient street food.
Traditional biscuit for the sandwich is the American "biscuit", which is flaky and savory, not a sweet cookie.
It is sometimes called a "pull‑ap" when served in small bite‑size portions at buffets.
Variations include adding cheddar cheese, fried onions, or pickles.
In some regions turkey or chicken sausages are used for a lighter version.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The sausage provides animal protein needed for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the biscuit and fats from the sausage delivers quick energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat products contain vitamin B12 and niacin, important for the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Sausage is a source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Calcium (when cheese is added)
items.content: If cheese is included, the sandwich gains calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Most ready‑made sausages contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Traditional sausages are rich in saturated fats, which in excess may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some sausages contain nitrites that can form potentially harmful compounds when heated.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The biscuit is usually made from wheat flour, making the dish unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of biscuit and sausage makes the sandwich calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be eaten hot, reheated in a microwave or skillet until the biscuit is golden. Add mustard, ketchup, mayo, or a slice of cheese if desired. For a lighter version use a whole‑grain biscuit and a turkey or chicken sausage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Keep sausages and biscuits separate: sausages in their original packaging or tightly wrapped, biscuits in a dry place. When reheating, ensure the sausage reaches an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

stewed-pigs-feet-puerto-rican-style.title: Stewed pig's feet, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed pig's feet, Puerto Rican style is a traditional dish from Puerto Rico made with pork feet slowly simmered in a fragrant sauce of tomatoes, garlic, onion, vinegar, olive oil, and characteristic spices such as adobo, oregano, and cumin. The result is a rich, slightly sweet‑sour flavor with melt‑in‑your‑mouth tender meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is often served at holidays and family celebrations.
In Puerto Rico it is sometimes called “cabeza de cerdo guisada,” although the feet, not the head, are used.
Long simmering turns the collagen in the cartilage into gelatin, thickening the sauce.
Traditional recipes add brown sugar or molasses for a subtle sweetness.
It is commonly accompanied by rice, beans, and fried plantains.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork feet provide high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Collagen source
items.content: The cartilage and skin are rich in collagen, supporting skin elasticity, joint health, and connective tissue.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc, and phosphorus are present, contributing to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Potential probiotic effect
items.content: Acidic cooking (vinegar) can foster beneficial bacteria that aid digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Pork feet contain a notable amount of saturated fat, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Salt and sugar
items.content: The traditional sauce is often salty and sweet, which may be problematic for hypertension or diabetes.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: Cooking challenges
items.content: Insufficient simmering leaves the meat tough and difficult to chew.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stewed feet hot, typically with rice, beans, fried plantains, or a fresh vegetable salad. The meat can be pulled off the bone with a fork and used in tacos, burritos, or as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweetbreads are the tender internal organs of young animals, most commonly calves (thymus sweetbreads) or lambs (heart sweetbreads). They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a delicate, almost buttery texture. Sweetbreads are a classic delicacy in haute cuisine, prepared by sautéing, braising, roasting, or turning into pâtés.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweetbreads are considered a delicacy in many cultures, including French, Italian, and Japanese cuisines.
The term “sweetbread” comes from the old French “sucre‑pain,” meaning “soft bread,” highlighting its tender quality.
Sweetbreads are rich in collagen, which makes them especially tender when cooked properly.
In traditional French cuisine, sweetbreads are often served with a mushroom‑and‑cognac sauce.
There are two main types: thymus (from the pancreas) and heart sweetbreads.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Sweetbreads provide high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and the formation of red blood cells.

items.title: Good source of iron
items.content: The iron in sweetbreads is highly bioavailable and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Contains zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Sweetbreads fit well into low‑carb and keto diets.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to animal offal.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: If not properly handled and cooked, sweetbreads can harbor harmful bacteria.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: People with elevated cholesterol should consume sweetbreads in moderation.

items.title: Liver concerns
items.content: Those with liver disease should consult a physician before eating sweetbreads.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweetbreads are usually trimmed of membranes, quickly seared over high heat, then braised in stock or roasted. They are often served as pâtés, sliced thin and pan‑fried to a golden crust. They pair well with lemon, herbs (thyme, rosemary), butter sauces, and mushrooms.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh sweetbreads in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic, for no more than 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in an airtight bag at –18 °C, where they keep quality for up to 3 months. Before cooking, rinse thoroughly and pat dry.

tuna-salad-made-with-light-italian-dress.title: Tuna Salad with Light Italian Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna salad with light Italian dressing is a ready‑to‑eat dish made of canned tuna chunks, fresh vegetables (tomatoes, cucumber, bell pepper), leafy greens and a light dressing based on olive oil, vinegar and Italian herbs. The meal is high in protein and low in calories, making it suitable for a light lunch or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the most popular canned fish thanks to its mild flavor and high nutritional value.
A light Italian dressing typically contains olive oil, wine vinegar, lemon juice and a blend of dried herbs such as basil, oregano and marjoram.
Tuna salad is a staple in many diet plans because it combines high protein with low fat content.
Tuna is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which support heart health and reduce inflammation.
In Italy, similar salads are served as “insalata di tonno” especially during the summer months.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Tuna provides a complete set of amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Help lower triglycerides, support cardiovascular function and reduce inflammatory processes.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Makes the salad suitable for weight‑control diets while providing a satisfying volume.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna is rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Tomatoes, cucumber and bell pepper supply vitamin C and lycopene, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tuna.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Mercury exposure
items.content: Regular consumption of large amounts of tuna can lead to mercury buildup; moderation is advised.

items.title: Oil in the dressing
items.content: Even a light dressing adds fat, so portion control is recommended for low‑fat diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The salad is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be enjoyed on its own, wrapped in a flatbread or pita, or used as a filling for sandwiches. For extra flavor, add fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a few olives.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package refrigerated at 0 °C – +4 °C. Once opened, consume within 2‑3 days. Discard if the smell or taste changes.
